turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mr. Harlan, come on back. I'll grab vitals before Doctor Shah sees you.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): About time. Uh, that waiting room chair is a joke and I'm not in the mood.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Dad, please. Sorry, he's short on sleep. I'm Karen, his daughter.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Right. Arm loose for me.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Blood pressure is 152 over 88, pulse 74, oxygen 98 percent on room air. Doctor will be right in.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): 152. Wonderful. Exactly what I needed today.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Morning, Mr. Harlan. I'm Doctor Shah. Karen can stay if you want. What brings you in?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): The cramps. Both calves, every night. I can't sleep and I'm sick of it.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): Nighttime cramps in both calves. How long has that been?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. Two months. Around when it got cold, I guess. Both of them, down in the calf.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): Every night, or just off and on?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Pretty much every night. Wakes me, I stand and walk it off. Couple minutes and I can lie down.
[SEG0013] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He paces the hall around two. I've caught it most nights I'm over there.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): Both calves, nightly, about two months, and walking helps. Any pain in the legs when you walk during the day?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Walking's fine. Not painful then.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any swelling in the ankles? Redness or warmth in the calves?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling. Not that either.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): What medicines are you taking?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): The water pill. Furosimide, forty milligrams, every morning. That's for my blood pressure.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Furosemide forty milligrams each morning for the pressure. So you've been told you have hypertension?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Years. They've called it hypertension the whole time. That's why the water pill.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hypertension, ongoing, on furosemide. Anything else, from us or from the store?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Magnesium. From the store, bottle says magnesium oxide, 400 milligrams. One at night for the cramps.
[SEG0024] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He grabbed it off the shelf last month. I told him to ask you, but.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): How much water do you drink in a day?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): The cramps are what I came for, not a lecture. They hit at like 2 or 3 and I'm up pacing. That's the thing.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll get to the cramps, I promise. The water, though, roughly how much?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): A cup with the pill. Maybe one more if I remember. I hate drinking cause then I'm up peeing. Not much.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): A cup or two, on purpose. Were you ever given a potassium pill with the furosemide?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Those horse pills, uh, K-Dur, twenty milliequivalents. I stopped it in March. They made me queasy.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Stopped the K-Dur twenty in March because of the queasiness. Did anyone ever give you quinine for the cramps?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. Nobody gave me that. I never took it.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): Okay, never took quinine. About the blood pressure. Any chest pain?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Never.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): Shortness of breath?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): Headaches? With hypertension, some folks get them.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes. Mornings, behind the eyes. Not every day.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): So not a flat no. Sometimes, morning headaches. Any dizziness, or a feeling you'll pass out?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Not that either.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm not asking if the hypertension is gone. You already said that's still there. Any blurry vision?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Pressure's still there, yeah. Vision, no. Not blurry.
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): And your stomach lately? Nausea, heartburn, any change in the bowels?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Stomach's fine now. Queasy was just those potassium pills, and I quit those.
[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me check the legs. Calves are soft, no tenderness, no redness, and I don't see swelling. Foot pulses are present, both sides.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm. Told you. Nothing in the daytime. Can we wrap this, I've had enough of sitting here.

[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): Almost. Let me read it back. Nightly cramps, both calves, two months, you walk them off. No daytime walking pain, no swelling, no redness. Hypertension on furosemide forty each morning. K-Dur twenty stopped in March. Magnesium oxide 400 at night. A cup or two of water. Occasional morning headache. No chest pain, not really short of breath, no dizziness, vision's okay. Fair?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Don't tack anything else on.
[SEG0049] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And he really does dodge the water. I've watched him slide the glass away.

[SEG0050] person_4 (DOCTOR): Furosemide can lower your potassium, and not drinking much can feed cramps like this. I want a blood test for the potassium, a basic metabolic panel. It's ordered, and the lab will draw it before you leave today.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. Just the needle, then I wanna go home. Don't hand me a jug in the lobby.
[SEG0052] person_4 (DOCTOR): No jug. Do drink more through the day, several glasses, not one cup. And stretch both calves before bed, hold it about thirty seconds each side.
[SEG0053] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back in two weeks to go over the panel. If the potassium is low we might talk about a supplement then, not today. Any drug allergies?
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No allergies. Two weeks, alright, let's just get out of here.

spec.situation: Older person with calf cramps at night for two months; takes a water tablet; drinks little water; magnesium from the shop; blood tests for potassium planned; stretching advice.

traps.happens: The patient denies some symptoms (said as 'no', 'not really', 'never'), has a chronic condition named earlier (for example asthma or hypertension) and later the doctor asks about another symptom of it, and one answer is a double negative or a correction ('not that either', 'no... well, sometimes').
traps.label_rule: Denials go in negative_findings with the exact thing denied, never in symptoms. NEVER write a negative about a condition the patient has said they have. A corrected answer keeps only the final version. A negative is never a symptom, and 'not painful' is the finding 'pain' absent, not a symptom called 'painless'.

features: patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

bad.reason: Patient said 'not really' short of breath, not a clear absence.
bad.text: Shortness of breath (status=absent, assertion=negative, reported_by=patient, temporality=current)

bad.reason: Dose and discontinued status supported, but indication potassium supplementation not explicitly stated.
bad.text: K-Dur (generic_name=potassium chloride, dose=20 mEq, indication=potassium supplementation, status=discontinued, reported_by=patient)
